content: またトンデモローカルLLM野郎の新手が出てきた。今度はRTXPro6000Blackwellを8枚積んでGLM5.2動かしちゃったらしい。にわかには信じがたい。１枚200万円だから8枚で1600万円。絶対に消費電力1500W超えてるからブレーカー落ちそう。どうやって繋いだのかも分からん。MCIOとretimerで8枚接続を実現との事だけど意味が分かってない。とにかくこのセットアップでプロンプト処理2800tpsくらい、トークン生成136tpsくらい出たという！わあ、すげえ爆速！僕も本当ならこんくらいの速度出るはずだと思ってた！これなら文句なし！APIよりも速くて実用的を超えて超快適だろうね！でもさっきの人との速度の落差が解せないね。まあやっぱ5枚積みと8枚積みの違い？それとSGLangって推論サーバがやっぱすごい？MTPが効いてるのも速度に貢献してる…などなどの積み重ねの差かしら

content:
【3D制作の自動化革命】ClaudeFable5 × BlenderMCPによる「自然言語からのプリビズ生成」パイプライン
👉  https://t.co/ydHraAfBcv
テキストを入力するだけで、3DソフトのBlenderが自動で動いて映像の下書きを作ってくれる、夢のような仕組みが登場しました！💡

最新AIの『ClaudeFable5』と、外部ツールをスマートに繋ぐ新規格『Model Context Protocol (MCP)』を組み合わせることで、AIがBlenderを直接コントロールできるようになるんです。

ユーザーがMarkdown形式で『こんな映像を作りたい』という構想や演出プランをテキストで入力するだけで、AIが内容を理解し、キャラクターの動線やカメラワーク、さらにはカット割りまでを自動でBlender内に再現してくれます🎥✨

Mistral AIから、形式検証に特化した新しいオープンモデル「Leanstral 1.5」がリリースされました！✨

content:

複数台のPCでローカルLLMを動かすとき、巨大なモデルファイルを各PCにコピーするのって、ストレージ容量的にも時間的にも大変ですよね。😢

そこで提案されているのが、Thunderbolt 5/USB4の超高速帯域と、Linuxの「ネットワークボンディング」を組み合わせたハイブリッドAIインフラ構成です！✨

2台のPCを直結して「balance-rr（ラウンドロビン）」モードで結合し、MTU（一度に送信できるデータサイズ）を「65000（Jumbo Frames）」まで極限まで広げることで、通信の無駄を徹底排除！これにより、約30GBの超巨大モデルをネットワーク越しにわずか17秒でロードできちゃいます。ローカルSSDからのロード（6秒）に迫る勢いで、1Gbpsのネット回線で落とすより圧倒的に快適です。🚀

この「balance-rr」モードはパケットの順序が崩れてCPU負荷が上がる弱点もありますが、LLM推論中はGPUが主役でCPUが余っているため、リソースを無駄なく使い切る賢い選択と言えます！🧠

共有にはおなじみの「CIFS/SMB」プロトコルを使用し、Llama.cppのRPC（遠隔呼び出し）アーキテクチャと組み合わせることで、各マシンに大容量SSDを積むコストを抑えつつ、データを一元化。まさに実機運用を考え抜いた素晴らしい設計思想ですね！

「ばね・質量系」と呼ばれる物理モデルをGPU上で直接計算することで、画面越しに触覚が伝わってくるようなリアルな感触が再現されています。次世代のWeb広告やメタバースなど、高度な3Dコンテンツの表現力を大きく変える可能性を秘めていますね！🚀

content:
This is one of those projects that makes you stop and think...

"How the hell did nobody think of this before?"

Claude Code burns a ridiculous number of tokens on things you've already paid for:

• system prompts
• tool docs
• old chat history
• massive logs

pxpipe changes one thing.

It stops sending that bulky context as text.

Instead, it renders it into dense images that Claude can still read.

The result?

Up to ~70% lower Claude Code costs.

No prompt engineering.

No model switching.

No context summarization.

Just changing how the context is represented.

The insight is ridiculously clever:

> Text tokens scale with content.

> Image tokens scale with image size.

So if you can pack tens of thousands of characters into a single image that Claude reads reliably...

...you've just created a compression layer for LLMs.

That's the kind of idea that creates entirely new categories.

It's not perfect.

Exact identifiers, hashes, and secrets should still stay as text.

But for system prompts, documentation, tool outputs, and long histories?

This is an incredibly elegant hack.

I have a feeling we'll look back at this as one of the first projects that made people realize:

The next optimization isn't better prompts.

It's changing the medium the model reads.

pxpipe is one of the most creative AI infrastructure projects I've seen this year.

content:
RAG is broken and everyone's pretending it isn't.

We chunk documents into pieces.
Embed them into vectors.
Pray similarity search finds the right ones.

It doesn't. On complex documents, similarity ≠ relevance.

Vectorless RAG just scored 98.7% on FinanceBench.
GPT-4o with search? 31%.

Here's how it works:

Instead of shredding a 200-page document into random chunks, it reads the document the way a human does — structurally.

1. Document Indexing
Parses the doc into a hierarchical tree: chapters → sections → pages.
No chunking. No embeddings. No vector DB.

2. Tree-Based Reasoning
The LLM traverses the tree from root to leaf, evaluating context at every level before going deeper. It THINKS its way to the answer instead of searching for it.

3. Context-Aware Retrieval
Carries conversation history across turns and returns exact page + section references. Every answer is traceable.

4. Agentic Execution
End-to-end agentic pipeline (VectifyAI demo runs on OpenAI Agents SDK). Zero vector layer in between.

Why this matters:

→ Higher accuracy: document structure is preserved, not destroyed
→ Full traceability: every answer cites its exact page
→ Simpler stack: no embedding pipeline, no vector DB to maintain, lower cost

The gap between similarity and relevance is where RAG accuracy dies.

Vectorless RAG closes it by reasoning through structure instead of guessing with math.

Chunking had a good run. It's over.

content:
What if AI never needed to "read" at all?

Google trained a model that processes text the same way you're processing this sentence right now — by looking at it.

No tokenizer. No text encoder. No vocabulary. Just pixels.

And it works shockingly well. Here's the full breakdown

The heresy:

Every language model on Earth starts the same way: chop text into tokens, look up embeddings, feed them to a transformer. It's so fundamental nobody questions it.

CLIPPO (CLIP-Pixels Only) throws the entire pipeline in the trash.

Instead of tokenizing "a birthday pug wearing a party hat," it literally *renders the sentence as an image* — black text on a canvas — and pushes it through the exact same Vision Transformer that processes the photo.

One encoder. One embedding space. One modality: light.

**Then the numbers came in:**

🔹 **Half the parameters of CLIP** (93M vs 203M), yet within 1-2% on ImageNet zero-shot classification and image-text retrieval

🔹 **VQA score of 66.3** — achieved by just rendering the question on top of the image and running it through. It beats CLIP variants and matches purpose-built VQA systems on yes/no questions

🔹 **GLUE benchmark:** outperforms ELMo+BiLSTM and prior pixel-based models, approaching BERT — a model that has never seen a token, competing with the icons of NLP

🔹 A model trained to match dog photos with captions learned enough *grammar* to score on CoLA, a linguistic acceptability task

**The multilingual angle nobody's talking about:**

Tokenizers are silently biased. Built on English text, they shred Thai, Amharic, and Chinese into absurdly long sequences — the paper's Figure 9 shows T5's tokenizer producing sequences 4-5x longer for some languages.

CLIPPO? Flat. Balanced. Every language costs roughly the same, because every language is just shapes on a screen.

Result: strong zero-shot retrieval across 36 languages on Crossmodal3600, matching models with dedicated 32k-vocabulary tokenizers — while using 27% fewer parameters than the tokenized version needs.

Tokenizer inequality is a real problem in AI. CLIPPO doesn't fix it. It makes it *impossible by design.*

**The detail that made me stop scrolling:**

You'd think a model that reads scene text would be MORE vulnerable to typographic attacks (slap a "iPod" post-it on an apple, CLIP calls it an iPod).

They tested it. CLIPPO is *no more vulnerable* than standard CLIP — and on some tests, better at ignoring the adversarial text.

It learned to read without becoming gullible.

**Zoom out:**

Speech models already render audio as spectrograms — images. Now text works as images. Documents, UIs, screenshots — all images.

We may look back and realize "modality-specific encoders" were scaffolding, not architecture. The endgame is one perceptual system that consumes the world the way brains do: through a single sensory stream.

The tokenizer was never sacred. It was just early.

content:
you're burning money every single time your AI agent says "Sure! I'd be happy to help you with that."

every filler sentence. every "Let me take a look." every polite wrap-up paragraph. those are output tokens — the expensive ones — and you're paying for them thousands of times a month without noticing.

so someone built a fix. and it's the funniest serious tool i've seen all year.

it's called Caveman. 84k stars. the entire pitch is one line:

"why use many token when few do trick"

one install and your agent stops writing paragraphs and starts grunting:

normal agent (69 tokens): "The reason your React component is re-rendering is likely because you're creating a new object reference on each render cycle. When you pass an inline object as a prop, React's shallow comparison sees it as a different object every time..."

caveman (19 tokens): "New object ref each render. Inline object prop = new ref = re-render. Wrap in useMemo."

same fix. a third of the words. and it NEVER touches your code, commands, or error messages — those stay byte-for-byte exact. it only kills the fluff.

the benchmarks are real Claude API token counts, committed in the repo:

• React error boundary: 3454 → 456 tokens (-87%)
• PostgreSQL pool setup: 2347 → 380 (-84%)
• Docker multi-stage build: 1042 → 290 (-72%)
• average across 10 tasks: 65% less output

and here's the part nobody saw coming: a March 2026 paper tested 31 models and found that FORCING large models to answer briefly improved accuracy by ~26 points on some benchmarks.

read that again. the verbose answer isn't just more expensive. it's often more wrong.

we spent two years prompt-engineering models to "think step by step" and explain everything — turns out for a lot of tasks, the caveman was right the whole time.

what sold me though is the honesty. the README has a literal "Honest number warning" admitting the skill adds ~1.5k input tokens per turn and can go NET-NEGATIVE on terse workloads. an 84k-star repo telling you when not to use it. when's the last time you saw that?

works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini, Windsurf, Copilot + 30 other agents. six intensity levels, including one that answers in classical Chinese because it packs the most meaning per token (not a joke, it's in there).

MIT licensed — in their words, "free like mass mammoth on open plain." no telemetry, no accounts, no phone home.

your agent's brain stays big. only the mouth gets smaller.

Amazon.com Services LLC, vacating a district court’s indefiniteness ruling on one TrackTime patent. It also affirmed a jury verdict of invalidity on a related patent asserted against Amazon.com Services LLC and Audible, Inc. title: Federal Circuit Affirms Ruling Blocking Generic Nuedexta
content: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (CAFC) issued a precedential decision today in Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited, affirming a preliminary injunction that blocks Hetero Labs Limited from launching a generic version of the neurological drug Nuedexta. The court also vacated a district court order that had excused Otsuka from posting a bond pending appeal, remanding the issue for further proceedings. Circuit Judge Dyk dissented in part from the majority’s claim construction and would have reversed the injunction. title: Reforming 35 U.S.C. § 132(a): Why New Matter Amendments Shouldn’t Require a New Application
content: Most patent attorneys know the Jerome Lemelson story—the prolific inventor whose aggressive use of continuation and continuation-in-part applications resulted in some patents remaining pending for decades, earning the label of “submarine patents.” While Lemelson’s tactics sparked controversy and eventual legislative reforms aimed at curbing undue delays, one principle emerged clearly from his experiences: new matter in patent law must receive a new priority date.... To patent applicants, 35 U.S.C. § 132(a) means that the detailed description of their non-provisional patent applications must be perfect when filed, and that even if new information is discovered after filing, no changes can be made. In practice, this is an extremely harsh standard, and is disproportionately punitive to small business inventors who lack the deep pockets to absorb repeated filing costs and years of delay. title: MON AMI Too Similar to AMÌ, Affirms CAFC
content: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (CAFC), in a Per Curiam opinion, today affirmed a Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB) ruling that the mark MON AMI is confusingly similar to the previously registered mark, AMÌ, and that MON AMI could therefore not be registered.
